subtype: Approach: rehearses a speech in the mind and in front of a mirror [Action]
passage: After school, Jahnavi stood in front of the tall mirror in the dance room, with her talk about honeybees due on Monday. First she closed her eyes and pictured the classroom: the teacher by the window, everyone sitting on the floor mats, herself beside the board. Then she opened her eyes and said her first line to the mirror. "Good morning, today I will tell you how bees talk without a single word." It came out smooth. The second point, how bees dance to show where the flowers are, vanished. She stopped, frowned and tried again. The same gap. So she stuck a note reading DANCE on the corner of the mirror. Varun, waiting his turn to use the room, peeked in. "Again?" "Again," said Jahnavi.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi's talk about?
qa.a: Jahnavi's talk was about honeybees.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when the second point vanished?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt frustrated and a little worried, shown by her frown and by trying again.

qa.q: What else could Jahnavi try to remember the second point?
qa.a: Jahnavi could practise with a friend listening, or draw a small dancing bee as a cue card, since a picture can help her remember.

qa.q: How might Varun see Jahnavi's rehearsal?
qa.a: Varun might find it funny that Jahnavi is practising again, but could also see that practising is how the gap was found.

grounding: Shows a girl imagining the room, rehearsing her opening line in a mirror and spotting where the second point slips away.

subtype: Approach: imagines the route and timings of an event day [Thinking]
passage: Sit down, Raghav. Manoj was sixteen once, you know. I had an interview for a scholarship in the district town, and the night before I lay on the mat and walked through the whole day in my head. Wake at five. Bus from the stand at seven. Get down by the market, walk ten minutes to the office, wait in the front room. I saw the bus, I saw the market. Then I saw myself in the front room opening my file, and it was wet. It had been raining for three days. I sat straight up. Nobody had told me, and I had never thought of it. So I woke Amma, asked for a plastic bag, wrapped the file and kept it under my shirt. My certificates stayed dry. Try it once in your head before any big day.

qa.q: How long had it been raining?
qa.a: It had been raining for three days.

qa.q: What did Manoj feel on picturing the wet file?
qa.a: Manoj felt alarmed and worried, sitting straight up, because nobody had mentioned the rain and the problem had never crossed Manoj's mind.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story protected Manoj's certificates?
qa.a: Asking Amma for a plastic bag, wrapping the file and keeping it under the shirt is what kept the certificates dry.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when woken for a plastic bag the night before?
qa.a: Amma may have felt worried but supportive, quickly finding a bag to help.

grounding: Shows Manoj picturing an interview day step by step and noticing no plan to keep the file dry.

subtype: Approach: imagines only the successful path and ignores obstacles [Pitfall]
passage: Swati here. I sat next to Devang on Thursday before our seminar. He was glowing. "I can see it," he said, eyes shut. "The slides, the pause, everyone clapping, Yamini ma'am nodding." He had pictured it every night that week. He never opened his slides on another laptop and never checked the cable. When his turn came, the projector showed only a blue screen. He froze with the pen drive in his hand, said, "It worked yesterday," and stood there for a full minute. Yamini ma'am asked whether he could talk without slides. He shook his head. I don't know what was in his mind. He only looked like someone who had never once pictured this.

qa.q: What did the projector show when Devang's turn came?
qa.a: The projector showed only a blue screen.

qa.q: What might Devang have been feeling as he stood there after saying "It worked yesterday"?
qa.a: Devang was probably shocked and panicked, and perhaps embarrassed, since he froze for a full minute, though Swati cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Devang have practised beforehand?
qa.a: Devang could have rehearsed a fallback, such as carrying a printed copy of the slides or practising the main points aloud without a screen.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt when Devang shook his head?
qa.a: Yamini may have felt concerned for Devang, wanting to help but seeing the talk could not go on as planned.

grounding: Shows a student imagining only a perfect, applauded presentation and having no plan when the projector fails.

subtype: Approach: simulates both success and things going wrong and prepares a response [Revision]
passage:
Seema: You used to say you just go on stage and it works. What changed?

Charu: A dead laptop, honestly. Two years ago mine died five minutes before a client talk and I stood there sweating. Now when I rehearse, I picture the good version, sure, but I also run two bad ones. One: the laptop dies. Two: someone asks, "Why is your number so different from last year?" For the first, I keep the slides on paper in my bag. For the second, I wrote a short answer on a card: what the number includes, and what I will check and send by evening. Last month the cable failed, I handed round the printouts, and nobody blinked.

Seema: And the tough question?

Charu: It came. The card was enough.

qa.q: What does Charu carry in case the laptop dies?
qa.a: Charu keeps the slides on paper in the bag.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when the laptop died two years ago?
qa.a: Charu felt panicked and anxious, standing there sweating five minutes before the client talk.

qa.q: What else could Charu prepare for?
qa.a: Charu could prepare for losing the slides file by keeping a copy on a memory stick or emailed to the host.

qa.q: How might the audience have seen the printouts when the cable failed?
qa.a: The audience might have seen Charu as calm and well prepared, since nobody blinked and the talk carried on.

grounding: Shows a presenter adding rehearsals of a dead laptop and a hard question, then carrying printouts and a prepared answer.

subtype: Approach: asks what if for the main risks and writes a plan B [Thinking]
passage: The village school's cricket ground was still green from last week's rain when Siddharth sat on the wall with his notebook. The match against the next village was fixed for Sunday. "What if it rains?" he said aloud to Nitin, who was tying the stumps together. "Then the ground is mud and we have called sixty people for nothing." He tapped his pen. "Plan B. I ask the headmaster for the verandah, carrom and kabaddi indoors, or he keeps next Sunday free for us." Nitin shrugged. "Rain isn't in your hands." "No, but the day can be," said Siddharth. He wrote both options down and walked to the headmaster's office before evening. By the time the sun went down, next Sunday was in the ground register with the school's stamp.

qa.q: Who was tying the stumps together?
qa.a: Nitin was tying the stumps together.

qa.q: What was Siddharth worried about?
qa.a: Siddharth worried that the ground would be mud and sixty people would have been called for nothing.

qa.q: What other backup could Siddharth add to his plan?
qa.a: Siddharth could send every player a message about the change by Saturday night, so nobody turns up to a wet ground.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Siddharth's plan B?
qa.a: Nitin might find it fussy at first, since rain is out of anyone's hands, but could come to see that it saves the day.

grounding: Shows a teenager asking what if it rains and arranging an indoor option and a reserved date.

subtype: Approach: prepares a backup for the likely thing that could go wrong [Action]
passage: Sit, Vaibhav. You want to know why I always carry two tickets? Let me tell you what Yash did at twenty. December, a banking exam in Lucknow, and every newspaper full of fog. I booked the night train, but I also went to the bus stand and bought a seat for later that night, and wrote both timings inside my ticket folder: train at nine, bus at eleven if the train failed. My friends laughed. The train was five hours late. Half the platform sat on their bags staring at the empty tracks. I opened my folder, walked to the bus stand and caught the last bus. I reached the city at dawn with time to wash my face. Two tickets cost me a little. Missing that exam would have cost me a year.

qa.q: What did Yash write inside the ticket folder?
qa.a: Yash wrote both timings there: train at nine, bus at eleven if the train failed.

qa.q: How did Yash probably feel when the train ran five hours late?
qa.a: Yash was probably worried but relieved, because the folder already had the bus timing ready.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story kept the exam from being missed?
qa.a: Buying the bus seat and noting both timings beforehand meant Yash could switch at once when the train failed.

qa.q: How might the other people on the platform have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt stuck and anxious, sitting on their bags without a backup like the one Yash had.

grounding: Shows a student booking a bus alongside a train and noting timings in case fog delays the train.

subtype: Approach: sets triggers for switching to plan B [Action]
passage:
Aditi: how many confirmations so far?
Usha: 43 as of noon 😬
Aditi: the big hall costs a lot if we half fill it. what's the plan?
Usha: I made a rule on Monday. if the count is under sixty by Friday 5 pm, we move to the small hall. no debate on the day
Aditi: and if it's 58?
Usha: then small hall. a rule only works if I don't bargain with it
Aditi: fair. I'll ask the venue to hold the small hall till Friday evening
Usha: 🙏 please. I don't want to be choosing chairs at 8 am on the day, tired and panicking
Aditi: makes sense
Usha: I'll message the speakers at 5:05 whichever way it goes

qa.q: How many confirmations had come in at noon?
qa.a: There were 43 as of noon.

qa.q: What does Usha worry about, and why make the rule now?
qa.a: Usha worries about deciding in a rush on the day, tired and panicking, so the rule is set beforehand.

qa.q: What could Usha add to make the rule work better?
qa.a: Usha could send a reminder to guests who have not confirmed, so that the count is closer to the truth by Friday.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel about holding the small hall?
qa.a: Aditi may feel reassured, since a clear trigger makes the venue request simple and avoids last-minute scrambling.

grounding: Shows an organiser fixing in advance a confirmation count and day that trigger a move to the smaller hall.

subtype: Approach: plans for so many scenarios that the main plan is neglected [Pitfall]
passage:
'Here it is,' Reena said, sliding a folder across the table. 'Twelve risks, twelve backup plans.'

'Even the one where the hall floods?' Kishore asked.

'Even that. Page nine.'

'And the demo? The main script for the demo?'

Reena looked at the folder. 'I'll do it tonight.'

'Reena, the client comes at ten tomorrow.'

'I know. I spent all week on the backups.'

The next day, after the client left, Kishore spoke quietly. 'The demo froze at slide four. We had no script for the normal path.'

'We had a plan for a flood, though,' Reena said, and rubbed both eyes. 'Nobody was ever going to ask about that.'

qa.q: How many backup plans did Reena write?
qa.a: Reena wrote twelve backup plans, one for each risk.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling when looking at the folder?
qa.a: Reena felt anxious and caught out, realising the main script was still not ready.

qa.q: What could Reena have done instead of covering all twelve risks?
qa.a: Reena could have chosen the two or three likely, costly risks for backup plans and spent most of the week preparing the main demo.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel about the frozen demo?
qa.a: Kishore may feel frustrated and worried, having asked about the main script the day before.

grounding: Shows a project lead writing backups for many unlikely risks and running out of time to prepare the main path.

subtype: Approach: prunes the list to the few likely, costly risks and revisits after each phase [Revision]
passage:
Vandana: Last year you told us you had twelve backup plans. What now?

Sangeeta: Three. I asked which risks are both likely and expensive if they happen: the supplier slipping, our lead developer being out, and the client changing scope. Each has a trigger. If the supplier's parts aren't here by the fifth, we order from the second supplier. If the developer is out two days running, we bring in the contractor.

Vandana: And the rest?

Sangeeta: Gone. And at every milestone we look at the three again. After the first phase the supplier risk was over, so I dropped it and added the test lab being booked out. A short list I actually read beats a long list I don't.

qa.q: What is the trigger for ordering from the second supplier?
qa.a: The trigger is the supplier's parts not being there by the fifth.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta want from the shorter list?
qa.a: Sangeeta wanted a list short enough to read and use, since a long one tends to be ignored.

qa.q: What could Sangeeta do if a fourth risk suddenly becomes likely?
qa.a: Sangeeta could add it with a clear trigger and drop or merge the weakest of the others, so that the list stays short.

qa.q: How might a team member see the shorter list?
qa.a: A team member might find it easier to remember and act on, since each trigger is simple and clear.

grounding: Shows a lead keeping three likely and costly contingencies with triggers, and reviewing them at each milestone.

subtype: Approach: leaves extra time before something starts [Action]
passage:
Tuesday. The bus stop was twenty minutes from Bhaskar's home, and he left at 7:40 for the 8:00 bus. Outside the temple, his classmate Mahima called him over to see a beetle. When he looked up, it was 7:52. He ran, and the doors were already closing. The conductor waved him in, and Bhaskar sat down, out of breath.

Wednesday. At breakfast his mother Kavitha noticed him staring at the wall clock. "I'll leave at half past seven," he said. "Ten extra minutes. If Mahima calls me again I can say hello and still walk."

Friday. Bhaskar left at 7:30, stopped by the temple to look at a new beetle for a few minutes, and reached the bus stop at 7:55 with time to spare.

qa.q: What did Mahima call Bhaskar over to see?
qa.a: Mahima called Bhaskar over to see a beetle.

qa.q: How was Bhaskar feeling as he ran for the bus?
qa.a: Bhaskar was worried and out of breath, afraid the bus would leave without him.

qa.q: What else could Bhaskar do if a friend calls him over again?
qa.a: Bhaskar could say he will look another time, or look quickly and check the clock first.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel watching Bhaskar plan this himself?
qa.a: Kavitha may feel proud and relieved that Bhaskar worked out the fix without being told.

grounding: Shows a boy leaving ten minutes earlier after a friend's chat nearly made him miss the bus.
